Al-A'mash related from Abu Zabyan, who said: "I heard Ibn Abbas say concerning His words ﴿as We sent down upon the dividers﴾: they are the Jews and the Christians."

﴿Who have made the Qur'an into fragments (idin)﴾: they divided it into parts and made it into limbs, believing in part of it and disbelieving in part of it.

Ikrima said: "They were called dividers because they used to mock, and some of them would say: 'This surah is mine.' Another would say: 'Mine is al-Baqara,' and another would say: 'Mine is Al 'Imran.'"

Mujahid said: "They are the Jews and the Christians, who divided their Book, separated it and scattered it."

Muqatil said: "They were sixteen men whom al-Walid ibn al-Mughira sent during the season of pilgrimage. They divided the mountain passes and roads of Mecca, and sat at its gates and entrances. Whenever the pilgrims came, one group of them would say: 'Do not be deceived by someone from among us who claims prophethood, for he is a madman.' Another group would say, by another way: 'He is a soothsayer.' Another group said: 'He is a diviner.' Another group said: 'He is a poet.' And al-Walid was sitting at the door of the mosque, whom they had appointed as judge. Whenever he was asked about the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he said: 'He speaks the truth' (sadaqa), 'for your saying' (li-waliyyika), 'the dividers.'"

Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: "They are a people who divided the Qur'an. Some of them said: 'It is magic,' some said: 'It is nonsense,' some said: 'It is a lie,' some said: 'It is poetry,' and some said: 'They are the tales of the ancients.'"

Some said: "They are those who swore an oath together against Salih and intended to kill him by night."

He recited the words of Allah: ﴿And in the city there were nine people who spread corruption in the land and did not reform, who said: 'Swear to one another by Allah'﴾ [al-Naml: 48-49], to the end of the verse.

﴿Who have made the Qur'an into fragments (idin)﴾: meaning, they made the Book of Allah, His Prophet, His command and His prohibition into parts, that is, they denied them.

As for His word ﴿idin﴾, some said: it is the plural of "udw" (part), and it is derived from their saying "'ada yu'dihi" when he divided it.

Ru'ba said:

"And the religion of Allah is not divided (al-mu'da)."

Meaning: divided into parts.

Another said:

"He divided the tribe of Banu 'Awf, and as for their enemy, he was content with him, and as for the honour among them, he was made to fail."

By his words "he divided me (adanni) Banu 'Awf" he meant: he insulted them and cut them off with his tongue.

Others said: Rather, it is the plural of "idah" (a part), it is said: "'ihah" and "'idin", like "yurah" and "yurin", "kurah" and "kurin", "qilah" and "qilin", "izzah" and "izzin". Its origin is "'ihhah," whose original letter "h" was dropped, just as they dropped the "h" from "shafah" (lip), whose origin is "shafhah," and from "shah" (sheep), whose origin is "shahah." The diminutive shows this: they say "shufayhah" and "ghuwayhah." The meaning of "'idhah" is lies and slander.

In a hadith: "Let none of you slander another."

﴿So by your Lord, We will surely question them all﴾ on the Day of Resurrection, ﴿concerning what they used to do﴾ in the world.

Anas related from the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning this verse, that he said: "Concerning 'there is no god but Allah.'"

Abd Allah said: "By Him besides whom there is no god, not one of you will be left alone with Allah on the Day of Resurrection, [just as one of you is alone with the moon on the night of the full moon], and He will say: 'O son of Adam, what deceived you about Me? O son of Adam, what did you do with what you knew? O son of Adam, how did you answer the messengers?'"

The heretics raised objections, with blinded sights and sick understandings, against this verse, concerning His words ﴿So on that Day, no one will be asked about his sin, neither man nor jinn﴾ [al-Rahman: 39], and they judged the two as contradictory.

The answer to this is what was related from Ali ibn Abi Talha from Ibn Abbas concerning His words ﴿We will surely question them all concerning what they used to do﴾ and His words ﴿So on that Day, no one will be asked about his sin, neither man nor jinn﴾. He said: "We will not ask them, 'Did you do such and such?' because He knows that better than they do, but He will say to them: 'Why did you do such and such?'"

Qutrub adopted this view and said: "Questioning is of two kinds: a question of seeking information and inquiry, and a question of rebuke and affirmation. His words ﴿So on that Day, no one will be asked about his sin﴾ mean a question of seeking information and inquiry, for He knew them before He created them. And His words ﴿We will surely question them all﴾ mean a question of rebuke and affirmation, to show them the power in punishing them."

Ikrima said: "I asked my master, Abd Allah ibn Abbas, about the two verses, and he said: 'The Day of Resurrection is a long day, and in it there are stations. They will be questioned in some of the stations and not questioned in others.' A parallel is His words: ﴿This is a day when they will not speak﴾ [al-Mursalat] [al-Anfal: 48, per the original]. And He said in another verse: ﴿Then, on the Day of Resurrection, you will dispute before your Lord﴾ [al-Zumar: 31]."

Some said: "﴿So on that Day, no one will be asked﴾ applies when the sinner is compelled and forced, and ﴿We will surely question them﴾ applies when they are acting by choice." It was also said: "No one is questioned if the sin was committed in childhood, madness, or sleep." The evidence is his saying (ﷺ): "The pen is lifted from three," and their saying: "We will surely question them" applies when their deeds were outside these states. It was also said: "No one is questioned if the sin was committed in the state of disbelief."

His words ﴿We will surely question them﴾ mean the believers. The evidence is His words: ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: if they desist, they will be forgiven what has already passed﴾ [al-Anfal: 38].

And his saying (ﷺ): "Islam erases what came before it."

﴿So proclaim openly (fa-sda')﴾.

Ibn Abbas said: "Make it manifest." Al-Walibi related from him: "Decide." Ata' related from him: "Do." Al-Dahhak: "Know." Al-Akhfash: "Separate." Al-Mu'arraj: "Distinguish." Sibawayh: "Decide."

﴿with what you are commanded (ma tu'mar)﴾, meaning: with Our command, "ma" being the verbal noun.

The original meaning of "sad'" is separation and division.

Dhu'ayb said, describing the donkey and the she-asses:

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 15, verses 87–99 (part 2 of 2):

And as if they were a lute (rababa), and as if he (the one who plays) ... the game of chance (yasr) that pours out over the arrows (al-qidah) and splits [them]. [Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 10/61; Lisan al-Arab: 1/406.]

[And it is said]: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was commanded to make the call (to Islam) public.

Musa narrated from Ubaydah, from his brother Abd Allah ibn Ubaydah, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) remained in hiding until the verse "So proclaim what you are commanded" (fa-isda' bi-ma tu'mar) was revealed, and then he and his companions went out openly.

Mujahid said: It means reciting the Qur'an aloud in the prayer.

﴿And turn away from the polytheists. Do not care about them. Indeed, We are sufficient for you against the mockers.﴾

God, may His praise be exalted, says to His Prophet (ﷺ): Proclaim the command of God and fear nothing except God. God is sufficient for you against whoever opposes and harms you, just as He was sufficient for you against the mockers. They were from Quraysh and its leaders, five men: al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah; Abd Allah ibn Amr ibn Makhzum, who was their chief; al-As ibn Wa'il ibn Hisham ibn Sa'id ibn Sa'id ibn Sahm; al-Aswad ibn al-Muttalib ibn al-Harith ibn [Asad] ibn Abd al-Uzza, Abu Zam'ah, against whom the Messenger of God (ﷺ) had prayed, saying: "O God, blind his sight and bereave him of his child" [192] [Jami' al-Bayan of al-Tabari: 14/94] ; al-Aswad ibn Abd Yaghuth ibn Wahb ibn Abd Manaf ibn Zuhrah; and al-Harith ibn Qays ibn al-Talatilah, who was a bowl-maker (?) ... [the text reads: "فإنه عيطل"; rendered here as "he was 'Ayṭal" (a name/epithet)].

Jibril (Gabriel) came to Muhammad (ﷺ) while the mockers were circling the House (the Ka'bah). Jibril stood, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) stood beside him. Al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah passed by him, and Jibril said: "O Muhammad, how do you find this one?" He said: "Wretched servant of God." (Jibril) said: "You have been sufficed," and he pointed to his shin and his hand. Then he passed by a man from Khuza'ah, an arrow-maker (nabbal), who was feathering an arrow of his, wearing a Yemeni cloak and dragging his waist-wrapper. A splinter from an arrow caught on his waist-wrapper, and pride prevented him from bending down to free it. He tore off his turban, and (the splinter) began to strike his shin and scratched it, and he became ill from it and died.

Al-Kalbi said: An arrow became caught on his garment and struck his main artery (akhhal), cutting it, and he died.

Al-As ibn Wa'il passed by him, and Jibril said: "How do you find this one, O Muhammad?" He said: "Wretched servant of God." Jibril pointed to the sole of his foot and said: "You have been sufficed." He had gone out on his riding beast with two (men) guarding him, and he descended into one of those ravines and stepped on a stone (sharqah), and a thorn entered the sole of his foot. He said: "I have been stung." They searched and found nothing, and his foot swelled until it became like the neck of a camel, and he died on the spot.

Al-Aswad ibn Abd al-Muttalib passed by him, and Jibril said: "How do you find this one, O Muhammad?" He said: "A wicked servant." (Jibril) pointed to his eye and said: "You have been sufficed," and he became blind [194] [Majma' al-Bayan: 6/133].

Ibn Abbas said: Jibril struck him with a green leaf, his sight was taken away, and his eye was in pain, so he began striking his head against the wall until he perished.

In the narration of al-Kalbi: Jibril came to him while he was sitting in the shade of a tree with his servant. He began to strike his head against the tree and to hit his face with thorns, and he called out for help to his servant. His servant said: "I see no one doing anything to you except yourself." He died while saying: "The Lord of Muhammad has killed me."

Al-Aswad ibn Abd Yaghuth passed by him, and Jibril said: "How do you find this one?" He said: "Wretched servant of God, though he is my maternal uncle." (Jibril) said: "You have been sufficed," and pointed to his belly, and his belly was split open, and he died at once [Tafsir al-Tabari: 14/97, with detail and variation].

In the narration of al-Kalbi: He went out from his family and the simoom (poisonous wind) struck him, and he turned black until he became like an Abyssinian. He came to his family, but they did not recognize him, and they shut the door against him while he said: "The Lord of Muhammad has killed me."

Al-Harith ibn Qays passed by him, and Jibril (peace be upon him) said: "O Muhammad, how do you find this one?" He said: "A wicked servant." (Jibril) pointed to his head and said: "You have been sufficed." He began to discharge pus from his nose, and it killed him.

Ibn Abbas said: He ate a salted fish, then thirst overtook him, and he kept drinking water upon it until his belly swelled and he died. That is the meaning of His words, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, We are sufficient for you against the mockers﴾, meaning (protecting) you and the Qur'an.

﴿Who set up another god with God, but they will come to know (their threat).﴾ And ﴿We know that your breast is constricted by what they say. So glorify the praise of your Lord﴾.

Ibn Abbas said: Pray, O Muhammad, to your Lord.

﴿And be among those who prostrate﴾, meaning the humble.

Al-Dahhak said: ﴿So glorify the praise of your Lord﴾ means: say "Subhan Allah wa bihamdih" (Glory and praise be to God). ﴿And be among those who prostrate﴾, meaning those who pray.

It is reported that when a matter grieved the Messenger of God (ﷺ), he would turn to prayer.

﴿And worship your Lord until the certainty comes to you﴾, meaning death. Its figurative sense: the one who is granted success by it.

Yunus ibn Zayd narrated from Ibn Shihab: Kharijah ibn Zayd ibn Thabit informed him from Umm al-Ala', a woman of the Ansar who had pledged allegiance to the Prophet (ﷺ), that they cast lots to divide the emigrants among themselves. She said: "The lot fell to us for Uthman ibn Maz'un, so we lodged him in our houses. He fell ill with the sickness from which he died. When he died and was washed and shrouded in his garment, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) entered, and I said: 'O Uthman ibn Maz'un, may God's mercy be upon you, Abu al-Sa'ib. My testimony concerning you is that God has honored you.'" The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "What makes you know that God has honored him?" She said: "I said: 'May my father be your ransom, O Messenger of God, then who (honors him)?'" The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "As for him, certainty has come to him, and by God, I truly hope good for him" [Tafsir al-Tabari: 14/101; al-Mustadrak: 1/379].

They said: When this verse was revealed, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "It has not been revealed to me to gather wealth and be among the merchants, but it has been revealed to me: ﴿Glorify the praise of your Lord and be among those who prostrate﴾, ﴿and worship your Lord until the certainty comes to you﴾" [195] [Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 10/64; Tafsir al-Tha'alibi: 3/409].
